daily_reality.summary: Orthopedic surgeons treat musculoskeletal conditions through surgery and nonsurgical care. Split between OR days (joint replacements, fracture repairs, arthroscopy) and clinic days (patient evaluations, follow-ups). On-call for trauma. Over 1.4 million hip/knee arthroplasties annually in the US.
typical_tasks: Perform total knee arthroplasty (TKA) and total hip arthroplasty (THA)
Fracture fixation — ORIF with plates, screws, and intramedullary nails
Arthroscopic surgery — ACL reconstruction, meniscus repair, rotator cuff
Spine surgery — disc herniation, fusion, decompression
Pre-operative planning with CT-based 3D software and robotic systems
Clinic evaluations — physical exam, imaging review, treatment planning
Emergency trauma call — fractures, dislocations, open injuries
Dictating operative notes and managing documentation in EMR

deadlines.board_certification_part_I: Taken in July after residency completion
deadlines.board_certification_part_II: Must pass within 5 years of Part I
deadlines.cme_requirements: Varies by state; AAOS provides up to 100 CME per annual meeting

daily_reality.seasonality: Joint replacements increase in spring/fall (patients prefer recovery during mild weather). Trauma is year-round but spikes in summer (outdoor activities) and winter (ice/falls). Sports injuries peak in fall (football season).

regulatory.summary: Board certified through ABOS (American Board of Orthopaedic Surgery). Requires 5-year residency after medical school. Subspecialty certifications available in sports medicine and hand surgery. State medical license required.

key_laws.name: ABOS Board Certification
key_laws.description: Part I Written Exam (320 MCQ in July) + Part II Oral Exam. Board eligible for 5 years after Part I.

key_laws.name: ABOS Subspecialty Certifications
key_laws.description: Orthopaedic Sports Medicine (est. 2007, 115 operative + 10 non-operative cases) and Surgery of the Hand (est. 1989)
key_laws.status: Active — eligibility recently expanded to post-Part I candidates

key_laws.name: State Medical Licensing Boards
key_laws.description: Require active state medical license for practice; renewal biennial

key_laws.name: ACGME Residency Standards
key_laws.description: Accreditation Council for GME sets training standards for orthopedic residencies

requirements: Medical school — MD or DO (4 years)
Optional: fellowship (1-2 years) — sports, hand, spine, trauma, shoulder/elbow, foot/ankle, oncology
ABOS Part I and Part II certification

regulatory.continuing_education: State-dependent CME requirements; AAOS annual meeting offers up to 100 CME credits; ABOS 10-year recertification cycle

tools.summary: Rapidly adopting robotic surgery (Mako SmartRobotics is market leader), computer-assisted navigation, and 3D CT-based planning. EMR systems central to workflow. Implant companies provide extensive technology platforms.

primary_tools.name: Stryker Mako SmartRobotics
primary_tools.description: 4th gen robotic system for total hip, total knee, partial knee, and spine. CT-based 3D planning with AccuStop haptic technology

primary_tools.name: Mako RPS (Robotic Power System)
primary_tools.description: New intuitive handheld robotic system for total knee — limited market release 2025

primary_tools.name: PACS (Picture Archiving and Communication System)
primary_tools.description: Digital imaging storage and retrieval — essential for pre-op planning and intra-op reference

primary_tools.name: EMR Systems (Epic, Cerner, athenahealth)
primary_tools.description: Electronic medical records for documentation, ordering, billing — significant time burden

secondary_tools: Smith+Nephew CORI Surgical System (robotic-assisted knee surgery)
3D printing for patient-specific instruments and guides
Dictation software (Dragon, M*Modal) for operative notes
pain_points: EMR documentation burden — 20+ hours/week on records
Prior authorization delays for joint replacements
High cost of robotic systems and implants
Learning curve for new robotic platforms
Supply chain issues for implants and instruments

terminology.summary: Extensive abbreviation-heavy vocabulary. Procedures, anatomical structures, and implant types all have standard shorthand used universally in OR and clinic notes.

terms.ORIF: Open Reduction Internal Fixation — fracture repair with plates/screws
terms.IMN: Intramedullary Nail — rod inside bone canal for fracture
terms.SLAP: Superior Labrum Anterior to Posterior (shoulder tear)
terms.DVT: Deep Vein Thrombosis — common post-op complication
terms.total: Joint replacement (slang — 'doing a total knee today')

career_psychology.summary: Highest-paid medical specialty. Extremely competitive residency. Long training (13+ years post-high school). 38% resident burnout rate. 60% of surgeons are 55+ creating looming retirement cliff. Strong career satisfaction despite demands.
career_path: Orthopedic surgery residency (5 years, highly competitive — ~3% match rate)
Fellowship (1-2 years) — sports medicine, spine, trauma, hand, joint reconstruction, oncology, shoulder/elbow, foot/ankle
Early-career surgeon (hospital employed or group practice)
fears: Surgical complications — infection, nerve damage, implant failure
Prior authorization denials delaying patient care
Physical demands declining with age (standing 6-10 hours in OR)
Student debt ($241,600 average total education debt)
motivation: Dramatic improvement in patients' quality of life
Technically challenging and varied surgical cases
Strong fellowship camaraderie and specialty pride
burnout_factors: Verbal abuse during training (3.7x burnout odds)
Work-life balance challenges, especially early career

community.summary: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons) is the world's largest musculoskeletal organization. Extensive subspecialty societies. Annual meetings are major professional events with up to 100 CME credits.

associations.name: American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons (AAOS)
associations.type: Primary professional association — world's largest musculoskeletal organization

associations.name: Subspecialty societies
associations.description: AOSSM (sports), ASSH (hand), SRS (spine), OTA (trauma), AAHKS (hip/knee), ASES (shoulder/elbow)

events: AAOS Annual Meeting 2026 — New Orleans, March 2-6 (up to 100 CME)
AAOS Annual Meeting 2027 — Las Vegas, March 3-6
Subspecialty society annual meetings (AOSSM, OTA, etc.)
State and regional orthopedic society meetings

market.summary: Highest-paid medical specialty with severe projected shortage (5,000+ by 2025). 60% of surgeons are 55+ creating retirement cliff. Robotic surgery adoption accelerating. Outpatient joint replacement projected at 51% by 2026.

job_outlook.retirement_cliff: 60% of orthopedic surgeons are 55+ years old
job_outlook.outpatient_trend: 51% of joint replacements projected outpatient by 2026

salary_market.highest_paid_specialty: Yes — orthopedics ranked #1 in physician compensation

demand_drivers: Sports injuries and active lifestyle demand
market_trends: Robotic-assisted surgery adoption accelerating (Mako, ROSA, CORI)
Shift to outpatient ASC (ambulatory surgery center) settings
Physician employment by hospitals growing (vs. private practice)
